doc.title: David Torkanowsky interviewed by Monk Rowe, New Hartford, New York, September 26, 2019

title: His solo piano, the Newport set and Herbie Hancock's voicings
summary: He critiques his own solo playing, recalls the Newport set and a lobby master class where Herbie Hancock showed 'Dolphin Dance' changes.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: What you’re describing obviously takes years of like preparation and knowledge so that you can —
So that you can let go and not have to think too hard.

I mean let me say this, my solo piano playing is pretty much the least interesting thing I’ve ever heard. You know like you hear Ellis Marsalis sit down and play, when he was filling in for Ellis Larkin at the Carnegie Lounge in Manhattan — just wonderful, flowing lyrical, delicate, grooving, swinging stuff. And you know I hear my solo stuff back and like for instance two years ago I did a solo piano set at Newport. And you know I just didn’t feel good about it at the time. As a matter of fact before the hit I got a call from The New York Times guy and he said, “Hey, man I’d really love to interview you about your upcoming Newport performance, how about if we talk right after the set?” So I finished the set and the guy came up and said, “Hey man, that was really good, listen I have another interview. Why don’t you just give me a call.” So I’m like cool, thanks. My solo piano is a work in progress. I’m not a huge stride player which, what am I doing playing with Evan Christopher. But I do have some unique New Orleansisms that are informed by my heroes like Dr. John, like James Booker, and I incorporate them into my playing, not in a considered way but it’s been infused. So I’m not thinking about anything. I didn’t even know what I was going to play. I was probably referencing in my mind that Dave Bartholomew moment when I started playing “Body and Soul.” ‘Cause Mac called me in, it was for Mac. So yeah, I try not to — sometimes I’m more abstract. I try to think of shapes you know. I mean Kenny Werner, Richie Beirach, you know, all these cats have come up with new harmonic approaches and I try to at least allude to that. One time I was in Mount Fuji jazz festival playing with Dianne and it was a monsoon typhoon outside. Everybody was jet-lagged, they were up in the lobby at two or three in the morning and Herbie and Mulgrew and a bunch of other cats, Herbie was doing a piano master class on the piano in the lobby. And somebody asked, “Herbie, man, what are those changes at the end of ‘Dolphin Dance’?” He goes, “Oh I used to play this and now I play this.” And it was like oh my God I never even thought about that. So I just, to this day I take those voicings that he showed me and try to you know, hear them without, oh I know what this is. I try to hear them. It’s difficult. But when I’m playing I try not to, I’m just trying to make it through.
Make it through. From point A to point B or skip B and —
Yeah. And I mean sometimes I’ll take a left and, oh wait a minute, and then I’ll go here. So it’s sort of a journey. It’s not evolved like I like, but I’m still working at it.
